Culture Tip (English): Many restaurants close between lunch and dinner (often around 3–5 pm) and stop taking orders 30–60 minutes before closing time ("last order"). A sign saying {準備中|じゅんびちゅう} (junbichū, "preparing") means the shop is closed for now; {営業中|えいぎょうちゅう} (eigyōchū) means it is open.

Popular places often have a line or a waiting list. You may be asked to write your name and the number of people on a sheet near the entrance (katakana or the Latin alphabet is fine), or to take a numbered ticket. Wait nearby until your name or number is called.
When staff say "Irasshaimase!" (Welcome!), you don't need to reply. A smile or a small nod is fine. Staff will usually ask how many people are in your group — you can answer by showing fingers, too.
In most restaurants, staff show you to a table. Wait at the entrance to be seated unless you are told "Osuki na oseki e dōzo" (Please sit anywhere).
Counter seats are common at ramen shops, sushi bars and small restaurants. When tables are full, staff may offer counter seats or ask if you are OK sharing a table (aiseki).

At food courts and many self-service cafés, people often save a seat before ordering by leaving a small item, such as a handkerchief, on it. Don't move other people's things. Never use a bag or phone to save a seat — keep valuables with you.
A teishoku is a set meal, usually a main dish served with rice, miso soup and small side dishes. It is a good-value choice at lunchtime.

Many restaurants have menus with photos, but English menus are not guaranteed. Pointing at a picture and saying "Kore o hitotsu onegai shimasu" (One of these, please) works well. Food models or photos in the window can help, too.

In casual restaurants it is normal to raise your hand and say "Sumimasen!" to call staff. If your table has a call button ({呼|よ}び{出|だ}しボタン, yobidashi botan), use it instead. In quiet or high-end restaurants, try to catch a server's eye rather than calling out.

Some restaurants take orders on a touch screen at your table or through a QR code on your phone; many have an English option. At many ramen, gyūdon and soba shops, you buy a meal ticket from a machine ({券売機|けんばいき}, kenbaiki) near the entrance and hand it to staff.

If you have a serious food allergy, tell staff before you order and ask about ingredients and cross-contact. Not every restaurant can check this, and some will say they can't accommodate allergies. A written allergy card in Japanese can help. A phrase alone does not guarantee that food is safe.

Many restaurants and cafés serve dishes only as they are on the menu, and changes may not be possible. Instead of asking staff to remove an ingredient, say what you can't eat and ask which dishes are OK — for example, "Nattsu wa taberaremasen. Dore ga daijōbu desu ka?" Removing an ingredient from a dish does not make it safe for an allergy.

Many Japanese dishes — soups, noodles, simmered vegetables and sauces — use dashi (soup stock), which is often made from fish. A dish that looks vegetarian may still contain fish or meat. If this matters to you, ask before ordering.
Many restaurants give you an oshibori (a wet hand towel) when you sit down. Use it to clean your hands before eating. Wiping your face or the table with it is considered poor manners in nicer places.

Many restaurants serve free water or green tea, and staff often refill it. At some places it is self-service — look for a water dispenser and cups. Free water is not available everywhere, especially at cafés; if you want some, just ask "Omizu, onegai shimasu."
Many people say "Itadakimasu" quietly before eating and "Gochisōsama deshita" after. They are not said to staff, and you don't have to say them, but they are a nice habit.
Slurping noodles is common and generally accepted at casual noodle shops, but you don't have to slurp.

Some eateries ask customers to get their own water, chopsticks or condiments, and to return trays and dishes. Look for signs saying セルフサービス (serufu sābisu, self-service), or watch what other customers do.

At self-service restaurants and food courts, you may need to return your tray and dishes to a return counter ({返却口|へんきゃくぐち}, henkyakuguchi) before leaving. At table-service restaurants, just leave everything on the table.

If your food is wrong or something is missing, calmly say "Sumimasen" and point at the problem. Staff will usually apologise and fix it quickly. Raising your voice is rarely needed and can make things harder.

At many casual restaurants, staff leave a bill slip ({伝票|でんぴょう}, denpyō) on your table; take it to the register near the exit when you are ready to pay. Other places take payment at the table, or ask you to pay first at a ticket machine. If you are unsure, ask "Okaikei wa doko desu ka?"
Paying separately (betsubetsu) is possible at many casual restaurants but not all, especially when it is busy. Ask before you pay.

Tipping is not expected in Japan. If you leave money on the table, staff may think you forgot it. Some restaurants add a service charge or a table charge to the bill instead; these are listed on the bill.

Many izakaya serve a small appetizer (otōshi) when you sit down and add a charge for it, usually per person. It is a seating charge, not a tip, and you usually can't refuse it. Ask "Kore wa nan no ryōkin desu ka?" if a charge is unclear.
Saying "Gochisōsama deshita" (Thank you for the meal) as you pay or leave is a warm way to thank the staff. "Sayōnara" is not usually said in restaurants.
Taking leftovers home is not always allowed because of food-safety rules. Ask staff first; some places will give you a container.

Some cafés ask you to find a seat first; others ask you to order at the counter first. At busy chain cafés, staff may say "Saki ni oseki o otori kudasai" (Please get a seat first). Follow signs or staff instructions.

Staff usually ask whether you will eat or drink in the café (tennai) or take your order away (mochikaeri / teikuauto). Prices can be slightly different because the consumption tax is lower for takeout. Bags may cost a few yen.
Many cafés use S / M / L, but some chains use their own size names, such as Short, Tall and Grande. Pointing at the size on the menu always works.

Many traditional coffee shops (kissaten) offer a "morning" (mōningu) until late morning: a drink with toast, a boiled egg or a small salad, sometimes for little more than the price of the drink. It is especially famous around Nagoya. Times and contents vary by shop.

At most chain cafés, you order and pay at the counter first. At traditional kissaten with table service, you usually order at your table and pay at the register when you leave — take the bill slip with you. Staff may ask if you have a point card; "Iie" (No) is fine.

At counter-service cafés, wait near the pickup counter and listen for your number, or watch the screen. Some cafés give you a buzzer that rings when your order is ready. At others, staff bring your order to your table.

At self-service cafés, sugar, milk, napkins and straws are often on a separate counter. Iced drinks are usually sweetened with liquid syrup (gamu shiroppu) instead of sugar. Some cafés only give straws if you ask.
Free Wi-Fi and power outlets are common at chain cafés but not available everywhere. Ask before using an outlet. Some cafés have a time limit when they are busy, often shown on a sign or the receipt.
At self-service cafés, bring your tray, cups and rubbish to the return station (henkyakuguchi) when you leave. At table-service cafés, leave everything on the table unless staff tell you otherwise.
At some cafés and food courts, you may need to find or reserve a seat before ordering. Follow the shop's rules and never move belongings left by another customer. Avoid leaving valuables unattended.
Ask about ingredients and cross-contact before ordering. Removing an ingredient does not guarantee safety.
